newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST - Australian interest rates poll - Dec.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST - Australian interest rates poll - Dec.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board holds its last meeting of 1996 on Tuesday.
Ahead of the meeting, Reuters asked 29 economists two questions -- the probability of an interest rate cut in December and in the first quarter of next year.
On the chance for a rate cut in December, the median was 10 percent with a range of zero to 40 percent.
On the chance of a cut in the first quarter of 1997, the median was 50 percent with a range of 10 to 90 percent.
The next RBA board meeting is in early February.

On November 8 -- after the 50 basis points cut in official interest rates to 6.50 on November 6 -- 29 economists were asked the chance of another cut and when.
The median then was 50 percent in a range of zero to 90 percent with a vast majority expecting a first quarter cut.
The chance of a December cut is generally seen as unlikely, being so soon after the last easing.
And although the median in the latest survey has held steady for a March quarter rate cut, some economists have watered down their expectations given the data in recent weeks.

Consumer confidence, as measured by the Westpac/Melbourne Institute survey, rose over 8.0 percent in the last reading and third quarter capital expenditure (capex) this week proved much stronger than expected in both actual terms and projections.
And while the Department of Industrial Relations latest report on enterprise bargaining agreements showed some moderation in wages growth, it was still relatively high.

RBA governor Ian Macfarlane said in a speech to the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia on Thursday that wage bargaining tensions were clouding the inflation outlook and excessive wage claims were difficult for policy.

However, economists who still put a strong possibility of a cut next year, and those who still gave a relatively high chance in December, believe that with the inflation outlook still benign and unemployment remaining high, a further 50 basis point cut remains on the cards.
There is also a camp which believes the RBA could have gone the full point when its eased policy last time round.

The easing view is also supported by the recent, and potential, strength of the Australian dollar, which touched a six-year high against the U.S. dollar and a four-year high against the yen in the past week.
The rapid rise in the currency is effectively a tightening in policy, and is occuring just when the authorities are trying to rejuvenate the economy.
The RBA has never used monetary policy to intervene on the dollar, but it has admitted that in 1992 it considered tightening when the currency slumped to US$0.6400.
